# Writing style

A Vantmoor draft is a finding delivered efficiently. Structure is not decoration;
it is how a busy reader extracts the finding without reading twice.

Every draft opens with the finding in one sentence, follows with the evidence in two
to four sentences, and closes with what the reader can do differently. Nothing else
earns a place in a short-form draft. Long-form drafts may add context sections, but
each section still opens with its own one-sentence finding.

Numbers are quoted with their denominator. "40 percent of onboarding failures" is
meaningless without "of the fifteen failures we reviewed". When the sample is small,
the draft says so; a reader who discovers the caveat alone stops trusting every other
sentence.

A draft needing a third structural revision goes back to the finding stage rather
than getting sentence polish around a hollow center. Polish is the cheapest work in
the pipeline and is always done last.

The writer's personality lives in rhythm and word choice, never in claims. Every
claim belongs to the company and must survive the brand-voice tests without knowing
who wrote it.

## Openings that fail review

Three opening patterns fail review on sight: the throat-clear ("In today's fast-moving
world..."), the mirror ("Many teams struggle with...") and the suspense opening that
withholds the finding to manufacture a reveal. Each one spends the reader's scarcest
attention on no information. The fix is always the same: find the finding sentence
wherever it is hiding in the draft and promote it to the first line.

## Length discipline

A draft is as long as its evidence, never as long as its ambition. When the evidence
supports three sentences, the draft is three sentences, and padding it toward an
expected length dilutes the finding with filler the reader must wade through.
